questions.question: Which statement about prokaryotic cells is correct? A Their ribosomes are 80S and are attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum. B Their cell wall is made of cellulose. C Their DNA is enclosed within a nuclear envelope. D Their DNA is circular and is not wound around histone proteins.
questions.answer: D: Their DNA is circular and is not wound around histone proteins.
steps: Prokaryotic DNA is a circular molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm and is not wound around histone proteins.
A is wrong: prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes and no endoplasmic reticulum.
B is wrong: bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan, not cellulose.
C is wrong: prokaryotes have no nucleus, so there is no nuclear envelope.

questions.question: An electron micrograph of a mitochondrion has a magnification of x18 000. The mitochondrion is 45 mm long on the micrograph. What is the actual length of the mitochondrion? A 0.25 um B 2.5 um C 25 um D 8.1 x 10^8 um
questions.answer: B: 2.5 um
steps: Actual size = image size / magnification.
A and C are power-of-ten slips when converting mm to um; D multiplies by the magnification instead of dividing.

questions.question: Describe how a digestive enzyme is made in a pancreatic cell and released from the cell.
questions.answer: mRNA is translated on rough ER ribosomes; the protein is carried in vesicles to the Golgi, modified and packaged, then released by exocytosis.
steps: The gene is transcribed in the nucleus and the mRNA leaves through a nuclear pore.
The mRNA is translated by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
The polypeptide enters the lumen of the rough ER, where it is folded.
Vesicles carry the protein from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi apparatus modifies the enzyme and packages it into secretory vesicles, which fuse with the cell surface membrane and release it by exocytosis.
accept: ATP from mitochondria supplies the energy for the process
The Golgi apparatus adds carbohydrate or otherwise modifies the polypeptide
Vesicles from the ER fuse with the Golgi apparatus
The vesicle membrane fuses with and becomes part of the cell surface membrane

questions.question: State two structural differences between a plant cell and an animal cell, other than the presence of chloroplasts in plant cells.
questions.answer: Plant cells have a cell wall and a large permanent vacuole; animal cells do not.
steps: Plant cells have a cell wall (made of cellulose); animal cells have only a cell surface membrane.
Plant cells have a large permanent vacuole (surrounded by a tonoplast); animal cells have none or only small temporary vacuoles.
accept: Animal cells have centrioles, which are absent from (higher) plant cells
Plant cells have plasmodesmata linking neighbouring cells
Plant cells contain starch grains whereas animal cells store glycogen granules

questions.question: Explain why the internal structure of a mitochondrion, such as its cristae, can be seen using a transmission electron microscope but not using a light microscope.
questions.answer: Electrons have a shorter wavelength than light, so the TEM has a higher resolution and shows the cristae as separate structures.
steps: Cristae are very small and close together, so seeing them separately needs a high resolution.
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.
So a transmission electron microscope has a much higher resolution than a light microscope (limit about 200 nm), and the cristae are seen as separate structures.
accept: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate points
In a light microscope image the cristae would be blurred together
A light microscope cannot resolve structures smaller than about 200 nm

questions.question: A student used a light microscope with an eyepiece graticule to measure a root hair cell. To calibrate the graticule, a stage micrometer with divisions of 10 um was used. 40 divisions of the eyepiece graticule lined up exactly with 30 divisions of the stage micrometer. Calculate the length, in um, represented by one division of the eyepiece graticule.
questions.answer: 7.5 um
steps: 30 divisions of the stage micrometer = 30 x 10 = 300 um.
300 um / 40 eyepiece divisions = 7.5 um per eyepiece division.

questions.question: One division of an eyepiece graticule represents 7.5 um. A root hair cell measured 24 divisions in length. Using this information, calculate the actual length of the cell, in um.
questions.answer: 180 um
steps: Actual length = number of divisions x length of one division.

questions.question: A student made a drawing of the root hair cell. The drawing is 63 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 180 um. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
steps: Magnification = image size / actual size, with both lengths in the same units.
63 000 / 180 = 350, so the magnification is x350.

questions.question: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from the soil. Root hair cells contain many mitochondria. Explain why.
questions.answer: Mineral ion uptake is by active transport, which needs ATP; mitochondria make ATP by aerobic respiration.
steps: Mineral ions are taken up by active transport (often against a concentration gradient).
Active transport needs energy supplied as ATP.
Mitochondria make ATP by aerobic respiration, so many mitochondria give a high rate of ATP production.
accept: Carrier proteins (pumps) use ATP to move the ions
A large supply of ATP allows rapid uptake of ions and maintains the concentration gradient
The Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation take place in mitochondria

questions.question: A sample of plant tissue has a water potential of -480 kPa. It is placed in a sucrose solution that has a water potential of -320 kPa. Which statement is correct? A Water moves out of the tissue because -480 kPa is a higher water potential than -320 kPa. B Water moves out of the tissue because the solution has a higher water potential than the tissue. C Water moves into the tissue because the solution has a higher water potential than the tissue. D There is no net movement of water because both water potentials are negative.
questions.answer: C: Water moves into the tissue because the solution has a higher water potential than the tissue.
steps: Water moves by osmosis from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to a region of lower (more negative) water potential.
-320 kPa is a higher water potential than -480 kPa, so the solution has the higher water potential and water enters the tissue.
A makes a sign error (it treats -480 as the higher value); B reverses the direction of movement; D ignores the difference in water potential, which drives net movement.

questions.question: Which statement about channel proteins in a cell surface membrane is correct? A They form a hydrophilic pore through which specific ions diffuse down their concentration gradient. B They use ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient. C They bind to a molecule and change shape to carry it across the membrane. D They form the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
questions.answer: A: They form a hydrophilic pore through which specific ions diffuse down their concentration gradient.
steps: Channel proteins have a pore lined with hydrophilic amino acids, so specific ions can diffuse through by facilitated diffusion.
B describes a carrier protein working as a pump in active transport.
C describes a carrier protein, which changes shape when it binds the molecule it carries.
D is wrong: the hydrophobic core is formed by the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids.

questions.question: Explain why oxygen can diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer of a cell surface membrane but sodium ions cannot.
questions.answer: Oxygen is small and non-polar so it passes between the fatty acid tails; sodium ions are charged and are repelled by the hydrophobic core.
steps: Oxygen is a small, non-polar (uncharged) molecule.
So it can dissolve in and pass between the hydrophobic fatty acid tails of the bilayer by simple diffusion.
Sodium ions are charged (hydrophilic), so they are repelled by the hydrophobic core and cannot cross the bilayer directly.
accept: Sodium ions can cross only through channel proteins or carrier proteins
Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient without needing a transport protein
The bilayer is a barrier to polar and charged substances

questions.question: Compare facilitated diffusion and active transport.
questions.answer: Both use membrane transport proteins; facilitated diffusion is passive and down a gradient, active transport uses ATP and can go against a gradient.
steps: Both use transport proteins in the membrane to move substances that cannot cross the bilayer directly.
Facilitated diffusion is passive and needs no ATP, whereas active transport needs ATP from respiration.
Facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient, whereas active transport can move them against it.
accept: Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins, but active transport uses only carrier proteins (pumps)
Both are specific to particular molecules or ions
Both have a maximum rate because the number of transport proteins is limited
The rate of active transport depends on the rate of respiration

questions.question: The concentration of glucose in the lumen of the ileum can fall below the concentration of glucose in an epithelial cell lining the ileum. Explain how glucose is still absorbed into the epithelial cell from the lumen.
questions.answer: Na+ is actively transported out of the cell, so Na+ enters from the lumen through a cotransporter that carries glucose in against its concentration gradient.
steps: Sodium ions are actively transported (using ATP) out of the epithelial cell into the blood, so the sodium ion concentration in the cell is low.
This creates a concentration gradient for sodium ions from the lumen into the cell.
Sodium ions diffuse into the cell through a cotransporter (carrier) protein that also carries a glucose molecule.
Glucose is therefore taken in against its concentration gradient, using the energy of the sodium ion gradient.
accept: Glucose then leaves the cell into the blood by facilitated diffusion
The sodium-potassium pump moves sodium ions out of the cell and potassium ions in
The cotransporter protein is specific to sodium ions and glucose
Microvilli increase the surface area for absorption

questions.question: A student investigated osmosis using cylinders of potato tissue. Each cylinder was blotted dry, weighed, left for 40 minutes in a sucrose solution, then blotted dry and reweighed. One cylinder had a mass of 3.20 g at the start and a mass of 2.88 g after 40 minutes in 0.40 mol dm^-3 sucrose solution. Calculate the percentage change in mass of this cylinder.
questions.answer: -10.0% (a decrease of 10.0%)
steps: Change in mass = 2.88 - 3.20 = -0.32 g.
Percentage change = -0.32 / 3.20 x 100 = -10.0%.

questions.question: A potato cylinder had its mass decrease from 3.20 g to 2.88 g after 40 minutes in 0.40 mol dm^-3 sucrose solution. Explain why the mass decreased.
questions.answer: The solution had a lower water potential than the potato cells, so water left the cells by osmosis.
steps: The sucrose solution had a lower (more negative) water potential than the potato cells.
Water moved out of the cells by osmosis, down the water potential gradient, across the partially permeable cell surface membranes.
accept: There was a net loss of water from the potato tissue
The solution had a higher solute concentration than the cell contents
The cells became flaccid (or plasmolysed)

questions.question: A student investigated osmosis using cylinders of potato tissue. Each cylinder was blotted dry, weighed, left for 40 minutes in a sucrose solution, then blotted dry and reweighed. Describe how the student could use this method to estimate the water potential of the potato tissue.
questions.answer: Use a range of sucrose concentrations, find the percentage change in mass of each cylinder, plot a graph and read off the concentration where there is no change in mass.
steps: Set up a range of sucrose solutions of different concentrations (for example 0 to 1.0 mol dm^-3), using the same volume of each.
Use potato cylinders of the same size from the same potato, kept at the same temperature for the same time, and blot dry and weigh each before and after.
Calculate the percentage change in mass for each concentration and plot percentage change against sucrose concentration.
Read the concentration where the line crosses zero (no net change in mass); the water potential of that solution (from a table or calibration curve) equals that of the potato tissue.
accept: Repeat each concentration and calculate a mean
Cut the cylinders with a cork borer so that they have the same diameter
Leave the cylinders long enough for equilibrium to be reached
Use the same balance for all the weighings

questions.question: The temperature coefficient, Q10, of a reaction is given by Q10 = rate at (T + 10) C / rate at T C. An enzyme released 24 cm^3 of oxygen in 60 s at 25 C and 36 cm^3 of oxygen in 45 s at 35 C. What is the Q10 of the reaction between 25 C and 35 C? A 0.50 B 1.3 C 1.5 D 2.0
steps: A inverts the ratio; B uses the ratio of the times (60 / 45); C uses the ratio of the volumes (36 / 24) and ignores the different times.

questions.question: A competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme-catalysed reaction. Which statement is correct? A The inhibitor binds to the enzyme-substrate complex and stops the product forming. B The inhibitor binds to the active site, and increasing the substrate concentration reduces its effect. C The inhibitor binds away from the active site and changes the shape of the active site. D The inhibitor permanently denatures the enzyme so that no substrate can bind.
questions.answer: B: The inhibitor binds to the active site, and increasing the substrate concentration reduces its effect.
steps: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate, so it binds to the active site and competes with the substrate.
With more substrate molecules, the substrate is more likely to occupy the active site, so the effect of the inhibitor is reduced.
A describes binding to the enzyme-substrate complex, C describes binding away from the active site (non-competitive inhibition) and D describes denaturation.

questions.question: An enzyme has an optimum pH of 7.0. Explain why the activity of this enzyme is very low at pH 11.
questions.answer: At pH 11 ionic and hydrogen bonds break, the tertiary structure and active site change shape (denaturation) and few enzyme-substrate complexes form.
steps: At pH 11 the (very low) H+ concentration changes the charges on the R groups of the amino acids in the enzyme.
Ionic and hydrogen bonds holding the tertiary structure are broken, so the enzyme is denatured and the shape of the active site changes.
The substrate is no longer complementary to the active site, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and the rate is very low.
accept: The tertiary structure of the enzyme changes
The substrate cannot fit into the active site
Denaturation at extreme pH is irreversible
OH- ions interact with the R groups of the amino acids

questions.question: Describe the induced-fit model of enzyme action and state one way in which it differs from the lock-and-key model.
questions.answer: In induced fit the active site changes shape to fit the substrate after binding; in lock-and-key it is rigid and already complementary.
steps: In the induced-fit model the active site is not exactly complementary to the substrate before the substrate binds.
When the substrate binds, the active site changes shape and moulds around the substrate to form the enzyme-substrate complex.
Difference: in the lock-and-key model the active site has a fixed (rigid) shape that is already complementary to the substrate.
accept: The change in shape strains bonds in the substrate, which lowers the activation energy
The enzyme is flexible in the induced-fit model but rigid in the lock-and-key model
Induced fit explains how an enzyme can act on a range of similar substrates

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the term activation energy and how an enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction.
questions.answer: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur; the enzyme holds and strains the substrate in its active site so less energy is needed.
steps: Activation energy is the minimum energy that the reacting molecules must have for the reaction to take place.
The substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The enzyme holds the substrate in a position or shape (straining its bonds) that makes the reaction easier, so the activation energy is lower.
accept: The enzyme provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
The enzyme brings two substrate molecules close together in the correct orientation
Activation energy is the energy needed to break the existing bonds in the reactants
Activation energy is the energy needed to start the reaction

questions.question: A student measured the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at five substrate concentrations, at 30 C and pH 7.0, with the enzyme concentration kept constant. The initial rates, in umol min^-1, at substrate concentrations of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 and 8.0 mmol dm^-3 were 12, 21, 32, 38 and 39 respectively. Describe how the initial rate changes as the substrate concentration increases.
questions.answer: The rate increases with substrate concentration (12 to 38 umol min^-1 up to 4.0 mmol dm^-3), then levels off at about 39 umol min^-1.
steps: The initial rate increases as the substrate concentration increases, from 12 umol min^-1 at 0.5 mmol dm^-3 to 38 umol min^-1 at 4.0 mmol dm^-3.
The rate of increase becomes smaller and the rate levels off, rising by only 1 umol min^-1 between 4.0 and 8.0 mmol dm^-3.
accept: The rate is not directly proportional to the substrate concentration
The curve reaches a plateau (maximum rate) at about 39 umol min^-1
The gradient of the curve decreases as the substrate concentration increases

questions.question: A student measured the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at five substrate concentrations, at 30 C and pH 7.0, with the enzyme concentration kept constant. The initial rates, in umol min^-1, at substrate concentrations of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 and 8.0 mmol dm^-3 were 12, 21, 32, 38 and 39 respectively. Explain why the initial rate hardly changes between 4.0 and 8.0 mmol dm^-3.
questions.answer: The enzyme is saturated (nearly all active sites occupied), so enzyme concentration limits the rate.
steps: At high substrate concentration nearly all the active sites are occupied at any moment (the enzyme is saturated).
Extra substrate cannot increase the number of enzyme-substrate complexes formed per minute because the enzyme concentration (number of active sites) is limiting.
accept: The maximum rate (Vmax) has been reached
Substrate concentration is no longer the limiting factor
Substrate molecules have to wait for an active site to become free

questions.question: An enzyme-catalysed reaction had an initial rate of 21 umol min^-1 at a substrate concentration of 1.0 mmol dm^-3 and 32 umol min^-1 at 2.0 mmol dm^-3. Calculate the percentage increase in the initial rate when the substrate concentration is doubled from 1.0 to 2.0 mmol dm^-3. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
steps: Increase = 32 - 21 = 11 umol min^-1.
Percentage increase = 11 / 21 x 100 = 52.4%, which is 52% to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: A student measured the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at five substrate concentrations, at 30 C and pH 7.0, with the enzyme concentration kept constant. The initial rates, in umol min^-1, at substrate concentrations of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 and 8.0 mmol dm^-3 were 12, 21, 32, 38 and 39 respectively. The investigation was repeated with a fixed concentration of a competitive inhibitor present. Predict and explain how the initial rates at 0.5 mmol dm^-3 and at 8.0 mmol dm^-3 would differ from the values given.
questions.answer: At 0.5 mmol dm^-3 the rate would be lower than 12 umol min^-1; at 8.0 mmol dm^-3 it would be close to 39 umol min^-1.
steps: At 0.5 mmol dm^-3 the rate would be lower than 12 umol min^-1.
There are few substrate molecules, so the inhibitor (similar in shape to the substrate) occupies many active sites and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.
At 8.0 mmol dm^-3 the rate would be similar to (close to) 39 umol min^-1.
The many substrate molecules are much more likely than the inhibitor to occupy the active sites, so they outcompete the inhibitor and it has little effect.
accept: The maximum rate is the same but is reached at a higher substrate concentration
At 8.0 mmol dm^-3 the rate may be slightly lower than 39 umol min^-1
The inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site
Binding of a competitive inhibitor is reversible

questions.question: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 28% of the bases are adenine. What percentage of the bases are guanine? A 22% B 28% C 44% D 72%
steps: Adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 28%, a total of 56%.
The remaining 44% is cytosine plus guanine, and these are equal, so guanine = 44 / 2 = 22%.
B equates guanine with adenine, C is the percentage of guanine plus cytosine, and D is 100 - 28.

questions.question: A single polypeptide chain contains 150 amino acids. How many water molecules are released when this polypeptide is formed from its amino acids? A 148 B 149 C 150 D 300
steps: Each peptide bond forms in a condensation reaction that releases one water molecule.
A chain of 150 amino acids has 149 peptide bonds, so 149 water molecules are released.
C assumes one water molecule per amino acid, A subtracts one too many and D doubles the number.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a triglyceride and explain how it is formed.
questions.answer: One glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds, each formed by a condensation reaction that releases water.
steps: A triglyceride is made of one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids.
Each fatty acid is joined to the glycerol by an ester bond.
Each ester bond forms between the -OH group of glycerol and the -COOH group of a fatty acid.
Each bond forms in a condensation reaction that releases one molecule of water (three water molecules in total).
accept: The fatty acids may be saturated or unsaturated
Each fatty acid has a hydrocarbon tail
The process is called esterification
A triglyceride is a hydrophobic (non-polar) molecule

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure and function of starch and cellulose.
questions.answer: Both are glucose polymers; starch (alpha-glucose, coiled or branched) stores energy, cellulose (beta-glucose, straight chains) strengthens cell walls.
steps: Both are polysaccharides: polymers of glucose joined by glycosidic bonds (formed by condensation).
Starch is made of alpha-glucose, whereas cellulose is made of beta-glucose (alternate glucose molecules are inverted).
Starch forms coiled (amylose) or branched (amylopectin) molecules, whereas cellulose forms straight, unbranched chains.
Starch stores energy (as glucose) in plants, whereas hydrogen bonds between cellulose chains form microfibrils that give strength to cell walls.
accept: Both are found in plants
Starch is compact and insoluble, so it does not affect the water potential of the cell
Starch is hydrolysed by amylase to release glucose, but cellulose is not digested by humans
Amylopectin has 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds

questions.question: Explain how hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges contribute to the tertiary structure of a globular protein.
questions.answer: Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges between R groups hold the folded polypeptide in its specific 3D shape.
steps: Hydrogen bonds form between polar R groups; they are weak individually but there are many of them.
Ionic bonds form between oppositely charged R groups; they are stronger than hydrogen bonds but are broken by changes in pH.
Disulfide bridges are strong covalent bonds between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine residues.
Together these bonds hold the polypeptide folded into a specific compact 3D shape, which is the tertiary structure of the globular protein.
accept: Hydrophobic interactions between non-polar R groups are also involved
The sequence of amino acids (primary structure) determines where the bonds form
Breaking these bonds (by heat or pH) denatures the protein
Hydrophilic R groups on the outside make a globular protein soluble

questions.question: A fragment of double-stranded DNA contains 1200 nucleotides in total. Thymine makes up 24% of the nucleotides. Deduce the number of nucleotides that contain adenine.
steps: Thymine = 24% of 1200 = 288 nucleotides.
Adenine pairs with thymine, so there are equal numbers: 288 adenine nucleotides.

questions.question: A fragment of double-stranded DNA contains 1200 nucleotides in total. Thymine makes up 24% of the nucleotides. Calculate the number of nucleotides that contain cytosine.
steps: Adenine + thymine = 288 + 288 = 576 nucleotides.
Remaining 1200 - 576 = 624 nucleotides are cytosine and guanine in equal numbers, so cytosine = 624 / 2 = 312.

questions.question: A fragment of double-stranded DNA contains 288 adenine nucleotides and 312 cytosine nucleotides. Adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds and cytosine pairs with guanine by three hydrogen bonds. Using these values, calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds between the two strands of the fragment.
questions.answer: 1512 hydrogen bonds
steps: There are 288 A-T base pairs: 288 x 2 = 576 hydrogen bonds.
There are 312 C-G base pairs: 312 x 3 = 936 hydrogen bonds.

questions.question: Two DNA fragments are heated until their strands separate. The fragment with the higher proportion of cytosine and guanine needs a higher temperature to separate its strands. Explain why.
questions.answer: C-G pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A-T pairs two, so more energy is needed to separate the strands.
steps: A cytosine-guanine base pair is held by three hydrogen bonds, whereas an adenine-thymine pair has only two.
More hydrogen bonds must be broken, which needs more energy (a higher temperature).
accept: The attraction between the two strands is stronger
A higher proportion of C-G pairs means more hydrogen bonds overall
Heat supplies the energy to break the hydrogen bonds
